# Statistical tests: what they are and when to use them

**What is a median? A mean?**
The mean is the sum of the values divided by their number. The median is the value that
splits the ordered data into two halves (50% below, 50% above). The median is robust to
extreme values; the mean is not [@manikandan2011].

**What is a variance? A standard deviation?**
The variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean (divided by $n-1$ for a
sample). The standard deviation (SD) is its square root, so it is expressed in the same
unit as the data. The SD describes the spread of the individual values; it should not be
confused with the standard error, which describes the precision of the mean [@altman2005].

**What is a normal distribution?**
A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution fully described by its mean and SD. About 68% of the
values fall within ±1 SD of the mean and about 95% within ±1.96 SD [@altman1995].

**What is a statistical test?**
A procedure that uses sample data to decide whether the observed result is compatible with
a null hypothesis $H_0$ (e.g. "no difference between groups"). It computes a test statistic
and the probability of observing a statistic at least as extreme if $H_0$ were true
[@greenland2016].

**When to use a statistical test?**
When we want to generalise from a sample to a population: for example, to decide whether a
difference between two groups, or between before and after a treatment, is larger than what
chance sampling variability alone would produce [@banerjee2009].
